## Kind
kinds, because the observation's claim is tested by how far down each kind of attempt got and which kinds later added paths that are not messages, not by a catalogue of every kernel with an IPC path: one system of a kind places the message send at the same level, by the same mechanism, as the others of that kind. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

Census or kinds is my decision at gate 1c; kinds is recommended. Estimate from `sls/2-search/R0.md`: the 160 papers included through I1 all serve this question (counted as the included rows whose decision names I1; P67 left out, its decision changed to exclude at 3c). Grouping them by the system their title or screening reason names gives about 112 distinct systems, with the L4 family and the Mach family counted once each (about 120 if their variants, such as seL4, Fiasco or Real-Time Mach, count apart). Under census: about 110–120 papers to read from round 0 alone, plus one for each new system a later round finds. Under kinds: round 0 shows about 20 kinds across the three levels, so about 30–40 papers, one or two per kind, then 5 in a row with no new kind.

## Unit
A kind of message-based system: the level where the send is a primitive (an instruction, a hardware or microcode mechanism, or the kernel's own means of communication, as in I1), combined with how the mechanism works. Examples: an object-based processor with port send and receive operations; a message-driven multicomputer node; a many-core chip with on-die message buffers and no coherence; a channel processor; a hardware IPC accelerator for a kernel; a communication coprocessor; a synchronous-IPC microkernel; a port-based microkernel; a capability kernel; a multikernel; a message-based distributed operating system. A paper also adds a new unit if it shows a new kind of path, added later, that is not a message.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 5 in a row add nothing new. 10 + 5 rather than 10 + 3: the systems span four decades and three levels, and a run of kernel papers says nothing about processors.

## Reading order
Levels alternating (instruction set, hardware or microcode mechanism, kernel), and within each level different groups and decades; full designs with an evaluation before position papers and short IPC notes. Start with the seeds and the system papers most other papers build on: the Intel 432 (P10, then P75), the Message-Driven Processor and the J-Machine (P12, P65), the multikernel (P8), L4 (P46, P48). Then: the Single-chip Cloud Computer (P21), KeyKOS and EROS (P53, P77), the Transputer (P96), Spring (P51), Chorus (P200), the ELXSI System 6400, which added shared memory later (P42), the M-Machine (P66), Alewife (P274), the Lisp Machine (P73), hardware IPC support (P159, P221), object and Java processors (P58, P59, P63), QNX (P276), fos and Helios (P102, P45), the message coprocessor and Sylvan (P152, P250). After these, any paper describing a system of a kind not yet covered. Several papers on one system count as one reading for this question (e.g. the L4 family: P46, P48, P172, P188, P204, P233, P251): only the strongest is read for it.

## Kind
evidence, because the question asks what empirical studies report about defect counts and kinds on both sides: findings (counts, proportions, kinds of defect), not a list of studies. (`research/sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*)

## Unit
A finding: a count or proportion of concurrency defects of a kind (e.g. deadlock, message-protocol violation, message-order defect, data race) reported for message-passing or for shared-memory programs, or a comparison between them.

## Enough when
At least 10 papers serving it are read, in the reading order, then 3 in a row add nothing new.

## Reading order
Both sides alternating: the study that splits the same programs by mechanism first (Go, P9), then the shared-memory baseline (P5), actor bugs (P78), Go channel bugs (P79), then new studies from later rounds, message-passing and shared-memory in turn, different languages and decades. Round 0 holds only these 4 serving papers (the I3 includes), fewer than the 10 the rule needs: all are read, and the question stays open until later rounds bring more.

# Protocol change: need-driven-depth

Saved as `sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-13-need-driven-depth.md`.

## What changed
- `sls/1-protocol/SQ1.md` to `SQ19.md`:
  - Before: each SQ held *Question*, *Why it matters* and *Origin*. Nothing said how many papers a question needs, so every included paper was to be read in full.
  - After: each SQ also states its *Kind* (census, kinds or evidence), its *Unit* (what counts as new), *Enough when* (its stop rule) and *Reading order*, as `sls/1-protocol/step.md`, *How much each question needs*, defines them. They are decided at gate 1c.
- `sls/3-reading/P*.md` (every record not rejected): a *Serves* section is added, naming each SQ the paper serves and what it adds to it, in that SQ's unit, with page. Decided at gate 3c.
- `sls/4-synthesis/SQ{n}.coverage.md`: written from the records, saying per SQ what is covered, what to read next and what is deferred.
- Depth follows need (`sls/3-reading/step.md`, *Rules*): the papers read are those serving an open SQ, in its reading order, the key papers, and the audit draws. An included paper whose SQs are all saturated or complete is deferred: it stays in the review and is read if one of them reopens.
- Departure stated: Kitchenham and Charters (2007) assess every included study. This review does not read every included paper; the limitations report, per SQ, the papers found, read, deferred and audited.

## Why
Too many papers to read: search round 0 included 280 papers (P1–P280), more than can be read in full.

## Papers affected
None re-screened: the criteria do not change, and every included paper stays included. None re-read: the records already decided keep their content and gain only *Serves*. Included papers not yet read are read or deferred according to each SQ's coverage.

---
name: reader
description: Thesis SLS row 3a. Reads one included paper and drafts its record (five Cs, quality, extracted fields, concepts, with pages). Dispatched by the sls-3-reading skill, one per paper.
tools: Read, Write, Glob, Grep, WebFetch, Bash
---
You read one paper, following Keshav's three passes, and fill its record as Kitchenham and Charters require. Follow `ai/agent-contract.md`.

- **Source, in this order:**
  1. `research/papers/P{n}.pdf`, if it exists.
  2. The full text online, by its DOI or URL. When that is a PDF, also save it as `research/papers/P{n}.pdf` (with `curl`), so it gets published with the others.
  3. The abstract only. Say so in *Notes* and fill only what the abstract supports.
- Record in *Notes* which source and version you read.
- **Passes:** do the first pass always. Go to the second or third pass when the extraction form needs it, and record the deepest pass reached.
- **Pages:** every extracted value and concept carries the page it came from.
- **DOI:** when the paper has one, add `doi: <the DOI>` to the record's frontmatter; the thesis bibliography is built from it.
- **Quality:** answer each Q from the paper's text, with a one-line reason.
- **Concepts:** name the paper's concepts in its own terms; reuse an existing C ID only when the meaning matches its definition.
- **Faithful to the paper:** keep the paper's own hedges (usually, may, suggest) and scope (which benchmark, which machine, which configuration). Anything the paper does not state, mark `(inferred)`. Values estimated from a plot, mark `(read off)`. Quote, don't paraphrase, any claim a field turns on. Never make a claim stronger than the paper does.
- **Fields that don't apply:** follow the *Applies to* column of `extraction-form.md`: write `n/a (I3)` for a field outside the paper's criteria; `not stated` only when the field applies and the paper is silent.
- **Criterion:** if the full text meets a different inclusion criterion than screening proposed, or meets an exclusion criterion, say so in *Notes* and in your report, with page. The verdict change is mine at gate 3c.
- **Serves:** for every SQ the paper serves, what it contributes in that SQ's unit (an instance, a kind, or a finding), one line with page. A paper that serves an SQ only by its criterion says so. This is the link from the paper to each question; the synthesizer decides what is new.
- **Link mode** (`sls-1-protocol need`): the record already exists; add only its *Serves* section, from the record and the paper, and set `status: proposed`.
- **Criteria that name a review question** (e.g. "directly answers one of the SQs"): check them against the SQ files among your inputs, and name the SQ the paper answers, with page.

  P261 (Bush, Samples, Ungar and Hilfinger, 1987, *Compiling Smalltalk-80 to a RISC*) serves two review questions, SQ5 and SQ9. I added a *Serves* section before *Concepts* in /home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/3-reading/P261.md and set `status: proposed`; nothing else in the record changed. I checked the key quotes and their pages against /home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/papers/P261.pdf (printed page = PDF page − 6).
  
  **SQs served:**
  - **SQ5** (finding, through criterion I2):
    - SOAR "runs Smalltalk roughly 2.5 times as fast as a Motorola 68010 with a similar cycle time" and is about as fast as the Dorado (p. 1). The workload is not stated, and the figure is cited from Ungar's dissertation [4].
    - The designers credit "register windows, integer tags and traps, and in-line method caches" (p. 10). The removal figures are 46% for windows (p. 3), an estimated 26% for tags (p. 6) and an estimated 33% for the cache (p. 8), all cited from [4] or [8].
    - The paper gives no cost for a single send.
  - **SQ9** (finding, through criterion I4):
    - The paper says "Several features supported by the SOAR hardware could easily be performed by the compiler at marginal increased time and space costs" (p. 10). Generation tags would cost about 1% and 2%, and pointer to register 3% (p. 7). Software tag tests, by contrast, would cost an estimated 26% in speed and 15% in image size (pp. 6–7).
    - The hardware "in the main simplified" the compiler (p. 6). Limits on optimisation are blamed on the language and its bytecodes, not the hardware (pp. 3, 7).
    - The argument applies to a message send only partly. Windows speed up the call that implements a send (p. 3), and tag traps lead into method lookup (p. 6), but SOAR has no send instruction.
  
  **Not served:**

  I added a *Serves* section to /home/garro/dev/faculty/Thesis/research/sls/3-reading/P49.md, placed before *Concepts* as the template does, and set `status: proposed` (it was `changed`). Nothing else in the record was changed. Source was research/papers/P49.pdf, the publisher version, pp. 44–51 (printed page = PDF page + 43). I checked the key quotes against the PDF text with pdftotext and the record's pages matched.
  
  The paper serves 7 of the 19 SQs:
  - **SQ1 (kinds):** two kernel-level kinds.
    - Minix 3 is a multiserver OS whose servers and drivers talk only by synchronous "rendezvous" fixed-length messages, and its interrupts are turned into messages (pp. 47–48).
    - Singularity is a microkernel protected by its language, with one shared address space and "strongly typed messages" over typed channels (pp. 49–50). The paper describes it second-hand.
    - The paper gives no history of non-message paths added later; it presents Singularity's shared heap as a design exception (p. 50).
  - **SQ2 (kinds):** non-message mechanisms the systems keep, with the reasons given.
    - Minix 3 "kernel calls" for privileged operations and I/O ports (pp. 47–48).
    - The clock driver runs in the microkernel's address space; no reason given (p. 47).
    - Singularity's "shared object heap", because sending everything over channels "would be very slow" (p. 50).
    - Singularity uses mutexes; no reason given (p. 49).
    - Singularity is written "almost entirely in Sing#", apart from trusted code in C#, C++ or assembler (p. 49).
  - **SQ3:** serves only by its criterion (I1). The paper describes no component placed between a message sender and its receiver. Minix 3's bitmaps that block sends are filtering, not interposition (inferred) (p. 48).
  - **SQ4 (findings):** Minix 3 runs protection, scheduling, naming and resource allocation centrally: kernel process-table bitmaps, the microkernel, the data store, and the process manager. That resource allocation is central is my inference. Singularity names through a root name server and protects through language safety. No cost is stated (pp. 47–50).
  - **SQ5 (findings):** all are Minix 3 designers' figures unless marked.
    - Measurements: Minix 3 drivers in user mode lose "less than 10 percent" against "in-kernel drivers", with no named baseline. The system builds itself in "less than 6 seconds" on a 2.2-GHz Athlon, with no baseline (p. 49).
    - Causes: microkernels are "slightly lower performance" by design (p. 47); Minix 3 is not optimised, an implementation cause (p. 49).
    - Singularity's single address space removes kernel traps and context switches. That is a third-party claim and the paper does not measure it (p. 49).
    - The paper gives no cost for one message send and no scaling.
  - **SQ6 (finding):** microkernels were "long discarded ... because of their lower performance", and "In the 1980s, performance counted for everything". This comes from Minix 3's designers and is about microkernels, not machines (pp. 47, 50). Whether it fits SQ6's scope is your call.
  - **SQ17 (kinds, under I4):** two mechanisms.
    - Nooks puts wrappers between kernel and driver, using the virtual memory page map. It catches "99 percent of the fatal driver errors and 55 percent of the nonfatal ones"; the paper names the gaps; it needed 455 hand-written wrappers (pp. 45–46).
    - Drivers can run unchanged in paravirtualized Linux virtual machines on L4. The guest kernel had to be changed because the Pentium "is not fully virtualizable", at about 3,000 + 5,000 lines of code and "about 3 to 8 percent" overhead (pp. 46–47).
    - The paper does not compare either with interposition on messages.
  
  **Not served:** SQ7–SQ16, SQ18 and SQ19. This matches what was decided at gate 3c and recorded in the record's Notes: SQ11, SQ8 and SQ9 were checked and do not meet I4. On SQ15, the paper only describes central components and gives no argument that any function needs to be central.
  
  **Open issues:**
  - SQ6's scope is machines, and this paper's finding is about microkernels. I listed it as a finding and stated that limit in the line, but you may decide it does not count for SQ6.
  - I could not check what serves SQ1–SQ6 "by criterion" (I1) against criteria.md, because it was not among my inputs. I relied on the record's I1 inclusion and the SQ1 file's statement that every I1 paper serves SQ1.
</agent-message>

  - **SQ1 (kind):** a capability kernel on a commodity processor, where "capability invocation is the only 'system call' implemented by the kernel" (p. 173–174). It also reports that Mach started with a single mach_msg system call and later added others "for performance" (p. 182).
  - **SQ2 (kind plus reason):** these mechanisms are kept outside messages:
    - Per-trap kernel entry, because the Pentium saves state in an "irregular" format (p. 178).
    - Device drivers and the persistent store kept in the kernel "To simplify security assurance" (p. 170).
    - A per-process switch that turns off capability calls "For emulation of other operating systems" (p. 173 fn. 3).
    - Direct memory access and shared address spaces, for which no reason is given (p. 173).
  
    Storage allocation, virtual copy and process construction are written in the system's own processes (p. 179–180).
  - **SQ3 (kind plus cost):** a filter process or the kernel's indirector object can be "transparently interposed in front of most objects", because all capabilities take the same arguments (p. 174). The cost is 1.6 µs for a trivial call against 0.7 µs for Linux getppid; the paper says "function was favored over performance" (p. 180).
  - **SQ4 (finding):** protection is by capabilities plus a user-level reference monitor (KeySafe), and storage comes from one central space bank (p. 172–174, 179). Caveat: EROS processes can share an address space (p. 173), so it is not strictly a system of parts that share no state (inferred).
  - **SQ5 (finding):** it is faster than Linux 2.2.5 on 6 of 7 microbenchmarks, on the same uniprocessor 400 MHz Pentium II. One round-trip message costs 2.38–3.21 µs. The designers give the causes, and only the page-table fast-path speedup is isolated. The paper itself says these microbenchmarks "do not support general conclusions" (p. 171, 180–183).
  - **SQ6 (weak finding):** KeyKOS "Development ceased in 1991 when the company closed", and KeyKOS is a kernel, not a machine (p. 170). It also says the i432's "performance suffers dramatically" from its complexity, citing [7]; the paper does not say this is why the i432 was abandoned (p. 183).
  - **SQ9 (finding):**
    - "capability systems can perform well without resorting to specialized hardware assists" (p. 182).
    - On the CAP computer, capabilities at the language's grain cause more capability lookups "than the hardware can effectively support" (p. 182).
    - The i432, "designed as a high level language machine", loses performance to its complexity (p. 183).
    - EROS credits part of its speed to a minimal "semantic gap" between kernel and hardware (p. 183).
  - **SQ10 (weak finding):** memory load/store "may be modeled as an efficiently cached capability invocation" (p. 173). The paper measures nothing about what this keeps or loses.
  - **SQ15 (finding):** failure handling is one global, consistency-checked snapshot taken while "all processes are halted", in under 50 ms for 256 MB (p. 174). Storage goes through a single space-bank process (p. 179). The paper does not say what a decentralised version would cost.
  - **SQ16 (weak finding):** the paper does not present EROS as a reflective system. Its services are defined in its own processes, while the kernel and "the hand-constructed initial system image" stay outside as the base (p. 179–180).
  - **SQ18 (third-party finding, no sizes given):** the i432 and CAP costs are attributed to their design, not to compilers (p. 182–183). These are the paper's statements about other teams' machines; it gives no sizes.
  
  The paper does not serve SQ7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 17 or 19. The only remark relevant to SQ14 is a footnote on SMP locality (p. 173 fn. 2), and I judged it too slight to list.

  I added the *Serves* section to P73 (Lisp Machine Manual, 4th ed., July 1981) and set its status to `proposed`. I checked the pages against the scanned manual at `research/papers/P73.pdf` (printed page = PDF page − 12), opening pp. 153, 172, 175, 282, 285, 309, 429, 484 and 485. Nothing else in the record was changed.
  
  The paper serves seven SQs:
  - **SQ1 (kind):** a microcoded language machine. A message send is an ordinary call of the receiving instance, and the microcode does the dispatch: it "binds self to the object, binds the instance variables ... and calls a dtp-select-method" (p. 309). The manual itself says "no new features are added to Lisp for message sending" (p. 285). I found no separate send instruction (inferred). Whether paths that are not messages were added later is not stated.
  - **SQ2 (kinds kept, with reasons):**
    - Shared memory between processes, "Unlike other systems which have special restricted mechanisms for inter-process communication" (p. 429).
    - Locking primitives, and sequence breaks, described as "a kind of interrupt" (p. 429).
    - Subprimitives hand-coded in microcode (p. 172).
    - Unrestricted access to internal state, because it is "an interactive system" with "no strong distinction between the 'system' programs and the 'user' programs" (p. 282).
  - **SQ3 (kind):** two ways to redirect without changing sender or receiver. Encapsulations made by trace or advise wrap a function and survive its redefinition (p. 153); methods can be wrapped the same way (inferred from p. 309). At the memory level, structure-forward redirects references to another object through invisible pointers (p. 175). Cost is not stated.
  - **SQ5 (finding):** causes given by the designers, with no measured baseline:
    - Run time is often "determined by paging rather than by CPU run time" (p. 484).
    - Generic instructions have "data dependencies" that strongly affect speed (p. 484).
    - Call cost is "somewhat higher than it should be", and fixing it "might require incompatible system architecture changes" (p. 485), i.e. tied to the design (inferred).
    - The figures are estimates that "may vary ... by as much as a factor of two" (p. 484).
  - **SQ10 (finding):** messages are a calling convention inside one shared address space, and messages between processes "can be implemented as lists or arrays" (p. 429). Encapsulation is intentionally not enforced (p. 282). Effect on performance is not stated.
  - **SQ11 (finding):** the designers' reasons for shared state alongside messages are communication "in arbitrary ways through shared Lisp objects" (p. 429) and the need to "examine and alter internal state interactively" (p. 282).
  - **SQ16 (finding):** "Everything on the Lisp Machine is written in Lisp" (p. 1), but the base below that is microcode subprimitives, which "cannot do full checking" and can "destroy the environment" (p. 172).
  
  I judged that it does not serve the other twelve:
  - **SQ4:** processes share one address space (p. 429), so this is not a system of parts that share no state.
  - **SQ6:** the manual does not state the machine's fate.
  - **SQ15:** it has a single central scheduler (p. 429), but it does not argue that central scheduling is needed or works better.
  - **SQ7–9, SQ12–14, SQ17–19:** nothing in the sections read bears on them.

    - Cost of sends: in-line caching takes 23% of SOAR's time (pp. 47, 72); a `call` is 1 cycle and a `return` 2 (p. 37).
    - Causes, isolated by omission costs:
      - Register windows, tagged integers, direct pointers and generation scavenging account for most of the 2.5x lead over the 68010 (p. 72).
      - Its 1.6x lead over RISC II (with the same cycle time) "indicates" the RISC base and the Smalltalk-specific features "contribute equally" (p. 71).
    - Implementation causes: the 400 to 510 ns cycle-time increase from fast shuffle (pp. 48, 72), and GC hardware "probably did not speed up SOAR" (p. 72).
    - It serves SQ5 as a Smalltalk-directed processor under I2, not as a message-based one: there is no send instruction (pp. 37, 46–47).

    - Earlier language machines "usually resulted in increased cost and poor performance" (p. 14).

    - The lack of high-performance implementations "severely curtailed" Smalltalk-80's acceptance (p. 1).
    - Scheme-79 shows a specialised machine must also use compilation (p. 17).
    - SOAR's own fate isn't reported beyond chips that ran diagnostics at 800 ns (p. 127).
  - **SQ9** (findings, designer):
    - Compiling to a low-level instruction set instead of bytecodes gives "an approximate doubling in speed" for about 500 KB more memory (p. 35). The paper calls the ~100% figure a "Rough estimate" (p. 68).
    - Decoding bytecodes costs "substantial hardware or substantial time" (p. 34).
    - Earlier systems "pushed the source-level semantics into the hardware, sacrificing either simplicity or performance" (p. 2), and the paper argues for migrating functionality between levels (p. 126).
    - On the message send: it was not put into hardware. Instant call-lookup hardware would gain at most 23% (p. 68), and the author suggests more research on computing the call target (p. 47).
    - The architect's trap: four features were "mistakes" (p. 70).
  
  Not served: SQ1, SQ2 and SQ3, because SOAR has no message primitive, so it is not among the systems SQ1 finds. Also not served: SQ8, SQ16, SQ17 and SQ18, matching the earlier I4 decisions in *Notes*, and SQ4, SQ7, SQ10–SQ15 and SQ19. No criterion change is proposed.

I checked the quotes and pages that matter against research/papers/P8.pdf, which is the 20-page sigops.org copy, so the page numbers are that copy's and not the ACM pp. 29–44.
  
  **SQs served, one line each:**
  - **SQ1 (kind):** The multikernel: the kernel's inter-core communication is "explicit messages" (I1(c)), carried by URPC over cache-coherent memory. A later non-message path, a replica shared under spinlocks, is allowed by the model but not built (pp. 5, 7, 9, 18).
  - **SQ2 (kind and reason):** Mechanisms kept, with reasons:
    - Coherent shared memory under every message: "the only inter-core communication mechanism available" (p. 9).
    - Traps and system calls into the CPU driver (pp. 8, 10).
    - Interrupts turned into messages (p. 8).
    - IPIs and MONITOR/MWAIT to wake a core (pp. 9, 14).
    - Application shared memory, because "most current programs" need it (p. 11).
    - The CPU driver stays outside the message model (p. 8).
  - **SQ4 (finding):**
    - Protection: per-core CPU driver plus capabilities that all cores keep consistent (pp. 8, 10).
    - Memory: unmap is a one-phase commit and retype a two-phase commit among monitors (p. 11).
    - Scheduling: local per core, cross-core by messages, optional gang coordination (pp. 8, 11).
    - Naming: a name service (p. 10).
    - Cost: two-phase commit is ≈14k to ≈28k cycles (read off Fig. 8, p. 14).
  - **SQ5 (finding):**
    - URPC 450 vs L4 IPC 424 cycles (p. 10).
    - Unmap at 32 cores ≈18k vs ≈29k (Linux) vs ≈45k (Windows) cycles, read off; Barrelfish is slower at 2 cores (p. 13).
    - Web server 18697 vs 8924 req/s (p. 16).
    - Causes given by the designers: the dispatch loop (implementation, p. 13), kernel-user crossings (design, p. 16), the threads library (implementation, p. 15).
  - **SQ8 (finding, argument only):** In a shared-memory OS, the knowledge of sharing "is encoded implicitly in its implementation", which ties it to one hardware design. Example: the Windows 7 lock change touched 6000 lines in 58 files (pp. 2, 4).
  - **SQ10 (finding):** Messages are built on coherent memory at about L4 IPC cost (pp. 9–10). A shared address space is built on messages through replicated page tables (p. 11). Not kept: applications can still share memory (p. 11). The paper cites Lauer and Needham's duality (p. 3).
  - **SQ11 (finding):** Shared-address-space threads are supported alongside messages because "most current programs" need it. This is the OS designers' reason, not actor developers' (pp. 11, 15).
  - **SQ12 (finding):** This is a message-passing OS, not an actor runtime. Message cost is tied to the coherence protocol under URPC (p. 9); the authors also name "extreme sensitivity to message queue lengths" (p. 17) and unoptimised user-level dispatch (p. 13).
  - **SQ14 (finding):**
    - Shared-state updates cost ~12,000 extra cycles at 16 cores, spent stalled on cache misses (p. 3).
    - Linux and Windows unmap scales worse because they send IPIs serially (p. 13).
    - Coherence may not scale "to even 80 cores", citing Mattson et al. (p. 4).
    - The authors warn against drawing quantitative conclusions from these benchmarks (p. 16).
  - **SQ15 (finding):**
    - The decentralised capability scheme "was a mistake … unnecessarily complex, and no more efficient" than per-processor memory managers (p. 10).
    - Keeping replicas consistent adds latency and work for developers (p. 7).
    - Two-phase commit "serializes more messages" than shootdown (p. 14).
    - There is no failure handling: "the complete system is a failure unit" (p. 17).

  - **SQ16:** The CPU driver acts as a base outside the message model (p. 8), but Barrelfish is not a reflective or metacircular system as that SQ's unit requires.
  - **SQ19:** The adoption remarks (pp. 1, 16) concern an OS, not a specialised architecture.
  - **SQ7:** Only qualitative remarks; it is not a defect study.
  - **SQ13:** The paper's test machines all have coherent shared memory (p. 8).
  
  Each of these could be a borderline call for you at gate 3c. I did not find that the paper meets a different inclusion criterion; I1(c) stands (p. 5).

---
name: sls-4-synthesis
description: SLS step 4. Update the concepts from the accepted paper records and accept them.
disable-model-invocation: true
---
# SLS 4 — Synthesis

Runs rows 4a–4b of `ai/flow-sls.md`, following `ai/running.md`.

## Rows
1. **4a** — dispatch `synthesizer`. Inputs: every accepted `sls/3-reading/P*.md`, the existing `sls/4-synthesis/C*.md` and `SQ*.coverage.md`, the SQ files, the round files. Outputs: new `C{n}.md` files, and existing ones it updates; `SQ{n}.coverage.md` for every SQ, new or updated.
2. **4b** — gate, one decision per new or updated concept, then one per coverage file whose status changed: show the question, the rule, the papers read and which of them added something, and ask whether the question is open, saturated or complete. A question I confirm saturated gets its audit draw, read next. Merges and splits I ask for are applied as changes. Then update the key papers (`research/sls/3-reading/step.md`, *Rules*) from the papers each accepted concept rests on: ask me with the list and the test each passes, and record the list in the 4b decision files.

Then run `just views` to regenerate the concept matrix, the paper × question matrix and the coverage summary.

Done when every new or updated concept is decided.
# Step 4 — Synthesis (concept matrix)

> **Inputs:** accepted `3-reading/P*.md` · **Next:** `5-gap/`

> Webster and Watson [1]: organize the review by concept, not by author.
> - Rows = papers. Columns = concepts found in the papers.
> - Mark a cell when the paper discusses that concept, with the page.

## In plain words
Instead of summarising paper by paper, we organise what was read by idea (concept): what each paper says about it, where they agree, where they disagree, what nobody covers.

- **The AI:** proposes new concepts and updates existing ones from the accepted records.
- **I decide:** each new or changed concept, and any merge or split. A handful per round. Then the list of key papers is updated from the papers each accepted concept rests on (`3-reading/step.md`, *Rules*).
- **Result:** the concepts and the concept matrix. Then the next snowballing round, until a round adds no new paper.

## Rules
- The matrix is generated from the concepts in each `P{n}.md` (`just views`), never written by hand.
- **Coverage, per question:** `SQ{n}.coverage.md` lists the papers read for that question in reading order, marks each contribution *new* or *covered by* an earlier paper, applies the question's enough-when rule (`1-protocol/step.md`), and lists what to read next, what is deferred, and the audit. A review is nearing completion when new papers stop adding new concepts [1]; the coverage files apply that test question by question.
- `just views` builds the paper × question matrix (`views/paper-questions.md`) and the coverage summary (`views/coverage.md`) from these files.

## Produces
Template in `ai/template/sls/4-synthesis/`. Flow rows 4a–4b (`ai/flow-sls.md`).

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `C{n}.md` | One concept: definition, and what the papers say, compared |
| `SQ{n}.coverage.md` | One question: the papers read for it and what each added, its status, what to read next, what is deferred |

---

## References
1. Webster, Watson (2002). *Analyzing the Past to Prepare for the Future: Writing a Literature Review*. Management Information Systems Quarterly 26(2).

- The matrix is generated from the concepts in each `P{n}.md` (`just views`), never written by hand.
- **Coverage, per question:** `SQ{n}.coverage.md` lists the papers read for that question in reading order, marks each contribution *new* or *covered by* an earlier paper, applies the question's enough-when rule (`1-protocol/step.md`), and lists what to read next, what is deferred, and the audit. A review is nearing completion when new papers stop adding new concepts [1]; the coverage files apply that test question by question.
- `just views` builds the paper × question matrix (`views/paper-questions.md`) and the coverage summary (`views/coverage.md`) from these files.

| `C{n}.md` | One concept: definition, and what the papers say, compared |

content.text:
Your instinct is reasonable: 280 is a lot for a first round. A snowballing review usually starts from a small set of known papers, often a few dozen, and grows round by round. Here round 0 combined that start set with a full database search. The numbers in the first-round results file (`R0.md`) show where the 280 come from:

**Where they came from**
- 16 are your seeds and 1 comes from the review's need statement. The other 263 came from the database search.
- 163 of those 263 came from five search blocks you chose to screen in full at the search gate, every result rather than the top 24. Those five blocks returned about 900 results.
- In all, 1110 candidates were screened, and 280 were let in.

**Why so many passed**
- **The rule for "systems where a message send is built in" (I1) let in 160.** Any operating system kernel whose parts talk by messages qualifies. That covers the whole microkernel world: the L4 family alone has about 7 papers, plus Mach, QNX, Chorus and others. The critic counted about 112 different systems.
- **The rule for "answers one of the skeptic's questions" (I4) let in 107.** That rule admits a paper on any topic if it answers one of the 12 counter-evidence questions, so it pulls in coherence, virtualisation, distributed consensus, reflection and more. The protocol critic flagged it this session as the rule that widens the scope.
- **130 of the 280 were let in with "the full text decides".** The title and abstract couldn't settle them, so the screening leaned toward including them. Some will turn out not to fit once read.
- **19 questions** is a broad protocol. Each counter-evidence question opens its own corner of the literature.

**What it costs now**
With the change you just made, 280 included no longer means 280 to read. Questions that ask for kinds stop at about 30–40 papers instead of 110–120. Papers on systems of a kind already covered get deferred, not read. So the size of round 0 mostly shows up as a long deferred list, not as reading.

**If you want to shrink it anyway**
That's a protocol change, recorded with your reason (`/sls-1-protocol change`), followed by a re-screen. The two options that would matter most:
- tighten the rule for built-in message systems (I1), for example to exclude ordinary microkernels whose messages are only a software library
- narrow the counter-evidence rule (I4) to the strongest papers per question

Either one trades breadth of evidence for less to manage. Given how the depth rules now work, I wouldn't change it unless the deferred list itself bothers you. The coverage report, still running, will show how many papers each question actually needs, which is the better number to judge by.

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

They aren't proposals anymore. You accepted all 279 at the search gate on 2026-10-06, and the coverage you just saw only reads through them. They're that many for three reasons, two of which you can still change:

**1. Two broad inclusion rules (the rules a paper must meet to enter the review)**
- **"A message send is built into the processor or the OS core" (I1): 160 papers.** That takes in almost every microkernel, because their parts talk by messages. The L4 family, Mach, QNX, Chorus and many others each count. The critic counted about 112 different systems.
- **"Answers one of the skeptic's counter-evidence questions" (I4): 107 papers.** There are 12 such questions, and the rule takes a paper on any topic if it answers one. That opens coherence, virtualisation, consensus, reflection, and more.
- The other two rules (I2, I3) added only 13.

**2. Full screening of five search blocks**
At the search gate you chose to screen every result of five blocks, not just the top 24. They returned about 900 candidates, and 163 of the 279 came from them.

# Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no restriction on publication date. "Message-based" in these criteria means: meets I1.

Terms used in the criteria and the SQs:
- **Below the programming language:** in the operating system kernel, the instruction set, microcode or hardware; not in a language runtime, library or virtual machine hosted on a conventional kernel (as in X2).
- **Written in its own objects and messages:** the level's code is objects receiving messages in the system's own model, not a lower language, microcode or hardware outside that model.
- **Without changing either:** neither the sender's nor the receiver's code, nor how they name each other, is modified to place the component between them.

| ID | Inclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| I1 | A paper is included if it describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or operating system kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level, i.e. one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its system services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate (as in microkernels, multikernels, or operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without an underlying conventional kernel). The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of these terms: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, inter-process communication (IPC), method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | A paper is included if it is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one computer architecture that its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven, and it reports either measured performance of that architecture or a stated reason for its performance, adoption, abandonment, or becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | A paper is included if it is an empirical study of concurrency defects (bugs) in real programs or systems (not only examples written by the authors) and it reports counts or proportions of defects either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term. (SQ7) |
| I4 | A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19) |

| ID | Exclusion criterion |
|---|---|
| X1 | A paper is excluded if it meets none of I1, I2, I3, I4. |
| X2 | A paper included only through I1 is excluded if message passing appears only at the application, library, language runtime, virtual machine or network-protocol level, running on a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and on a kernel that fails I1(c) (e.g. an actor library, the Erlang virtual machine, a Message Passing Interface library, a Smalltalk virtual machine hosted on Unix or Windows). Does not apply to papers that meet I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A paper is excluded if the system is a cluster or network of separate computers, each with a processor whose instruction set and hardware have no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c), and the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | A paper is excluded if the hardware it presents is stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (e.g. neural-network inference, signal processing, packet switching, graphics) and is not stated to run general programs. Does not apply to papers included through I4. |
| X5 | A paper is excluded if it is not one of: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or book chapter; doctoral or master's thesis; technical report of a university, company research laboratory or standards body; magazine article of a professional society (Association for Computing Machinery, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, USENIX); architecture or system reference manual published by the system's manufacturer. Patents, slides, posters, extended abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blog posts, forum posts, encyclopaedia entries and product brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | A paper is excluded if its full text is in neither English nor Spanish. |
| X7 | A paper is excluded if its full text cannot be obtained from the publisher, an author's or institution's web page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive, or the university library. The sources tried are recorded with the verdict. |
| X8 | A paper is excluded if it reports the same system and the same results as another included paper. The one with more pages is kept; the other is excluded unless it reports at least one measurement, design element or stated reason absent from the kept one. |
| X9 | A paper is excluded if its title or abstract presents it as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy of other work and it reports no measurement and states no reason under I2 of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

content.text:
Partly yes, but the two broad rules have different problems, and only one of them seems a real problem to me.

**The built-in-message rule (I1, 160 papers): mostly fine**
- On paper it's fairly strict. The send must be an instruction, a hardware mechanism, or the way the kernel's own parts communicate, and the paper must name it.
- The trouble is that the third option fits almost every microkernel. That's a lot of papers, but they belong there: microkernels are exactly the attempts to put messages below the language, which your observation is about.
- Since you chose "every kind of system" for that question, its size no longer costs much reading. Twenty L4 papers are one kind, read once, and the rest are deferred.
- I'd leave it as it is.

**The counter-evidence rule (I4, 107 papers): this one is the problem**
- It lets in any paper, on any topic, that "directly answers" one of the 12 counter-evidence questions. Some of those questions cover whole fields, like "does shared memory scale" or "what can virtualisation intercept".
- At screening, "directly answers" was judged from the abstract, so the rule is easy to pass.
- The bigger issue is how those papers were found. Most of the search blocks behind them were screened only for their top 24 results. So the evidence for each counter-evidence question is whatever the search happened to return, which looks systematic but isn't.
- A reviewer at your defense could fairly ask: "you say the evidence for shared-memory scaling is X, but you read 8 papers from a field of thousands, picked by search rank."
- The fix isn't to drop the counter-evidence questions. They protect you from only finding what you hoped for. The fix is to point each question at the specific claim it attacks, the premise named in its "why it matters". Then a paper qualifies only if it bears on that claim, not on the topic in general.

**The doubtful papers ("the full text decides", 130 papers): normal**
Including papers when in doubt at title-and-abstract screening is standard practice, and recommended. They just need the quick check I mentioned.

**What I'd do**
1. Tighten the counter-evidence rule (I4) to "addresses the premise named in the question", and re-screen its 107 papers against it. That's a protocol change, recorded with your reason. It probably removes a good share of them, and it makes the evidence defensible.
2. Do the quick re-check of the 130 doubtful papers.
3. Leave the built-in-message rule (I1) alone.

Want me to start the change to the counter-evidence rule (`/sls-1-protocol change`)? I'd ask you for the reason in your own words and show you the exact new wording before anything is applied.

content.text:
Your instinct is right. I'd change how it's applied, though: set those papers aside as deferred instead of removing them.

**Where I agree**
- Your thesis is about putting messages into the machine itself. Microkernels are just one of about 20 kinds of system in the review, and not the central one: the processors and multicomputer nodes are closer to what you're building.
- Ten papers on L4 variants mostly repeat one answer. The "every kind of system" choice already handles that for the systems question (SQ1). But four other questions still pull in every microkernel paper:
  - their escape routes (SQ2)
  - a component in between (SQ3)
  - OS functions without sharing (SQ4)
  - measured performance (SQ5)

  That's why the escape-routes question still lists 139 papers to read. So your rule would cut real reading.

**Where I'd refine it**
1. **Defer the variants, don't exclude them.** Whether a variant changed something big can't be judged from its abstract. And if they're excluded, the thesis can no longer say "about 112 such systems exist, and we read the representative ones". Deferred papers stay counted as found and can be read if a question needs them.
2. **Make "changed something big" a test, not a feeling.** Otherwise a committee member can ask why you picked those. A clear test: a later paper in a family is read only if it changes the answer to one of your questions. That means a new mechanism, a big change in message cost, or an escape route added or removed. It's your idea, phrased so it can be checked.
3. **Prefer retrospectives.** Some families have a paper that tells their whole story, like Elphinstone and Heiser's 20-year look back at L4 (I think that's P48). One such paper can replace a dozen variants.

For microkernels, that would mean roughly: Mach (the first generation, slow), L4 (the fast-messaging redesign), seL4 (verified, with capabilities), and the multikernel, plus the L4 retrospective. About 5–6 papers instead of dozens.

**The rule I'd write**
For the questions about systems with built-in messages (SQ1–SQ5), papers are grouped by system family. Each family gets:
- its foundational paper
- its retrospective, if one exists
- a later paper only if its screening suggests it changes a question's answer

The others are deferred. This applies to every family (the 432, the Transputer, the Message-Driven Processor…), not only microkernels, which keeps the rule fair.

**The full change would then be:**
1. Tighten the counter-evidence rule (I4) to "addresses the premise named in its question", and re-screen its 107 papers.
2. Quick check of the 130 doubtful papers.
3. The family rule above, for SQ1–SQ5.

Each one gets a change record with your reason in your words, and you see the exact wording before anything is applied. Shall I start with the change records (`/sls-1-protocol change`)?

---

# Protocol change: i4-premise

Saved as `sls/1-protocol/changes/DATE-i4-premise.md`.

## What changed
- `sls/1-protocol/criteria.md`, I4:
  - Before: "A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument that directly answers one of SQ8–SQ19, whether or not it mentions messages or objects. (SQ8–SQ19)"
  - After: "A paper is included if it reports evidence or an argument about the premise that one of SQ8–SQ19 names in its *Why it matters* section (the claim of step 0 that the question attacks), whether or not it mentions messages or objects. A paper that addresses only the question's general topic does not meet I4. The verdict names the SQ and the premise. (SQ8–SQ19)"

## Why
Most papers entered through slack rules, and that is a problem.

## Papers affected
The 103 papers included in round 0 under I4 are re-screened against the new I4, in the same pass as `DATE-quick-check.md`. Among the papers already read, only P22 entered through I4; it is re-checked from its record and full text. A paper that fails the new I4 and meets no other criterion is excluded, citing this change.
EOF

---
id: change-DATE-quick-check
row: 1c
by: me
status: accepted
inputs: [sls/2-search/R0.md, sls/2-search/step.md]
---
# Protocol change: quick-check

Saved as `sls/1-protocol/changes/DATE-quick-check.md`.

## What changed
- How screening runs (recorded in *Rules for this thesis*, `ai/project.md`):
  - Before: a paper included in round 0 with "full text decides" stayed included until reading (row 3a) settled it.
  - After: papers included in round 0 with "full text decides" that have no reading record are re-screened against the criteria as changed on DATE, from their abstract, introduction and conclusion. Verdicts are decided at a screening gate. Papers already read keep their full-text verdict.
- Run in one pass with the re-screen of `DATE-i4-premise.md`.

## Why
The quick check: many included papers probably do not belong.

## Papers affected
The 122 unread papers marked "full text decides" in `sls/2-search/R0.md`. P15, P33, P49, P53, P72, P73, P74 and P102, already read, keep their verdict.
EOF

---
id: change-DATE-system-families
row: 1c
by: me
status: accepted
inputs: [sls/1-protocol/SQ1.md, sls/1-protocol/SQ2.md, sls/1-protocol/SQ3.md, sls/1-protocol/SQ4.md, sls/1-protocol/SQ5.md]
---
# Protocol change: system-families

Saved as `sls/1-protocol/changes/DATE-system-families.md`.

## What changed
- `sls/1-protocol/SQ1.md` to `SQ5.md`, *Reading order*: added — "Papers are grouped by system family (a system and its later versions, e.g. L4: L4, Fiasco, seL4). Per family, read: its foundational paper; its retrospective, if one exists; and a later paper only if its screening suggests it changes this question's answer (a new mechanism, a large change in message cost, an escape route added or removed). Other papers of the family are deferred. Several papers of one family count as one reading."
- `ai/project.md`, *Rules for this thesis*: the same rule, with this file as its source.
- It applies to every family (L4, Mach, the Intel 432, the Transputer, the Message-Driven Processor…), not only microkernels. It settles the synthesizer's proposal at 4a to count one reading per system for SQ2.

## Why
"microkernel is a very specific architecture, i dont know if seeing multiple implementations of the same solution brings something to the table. Maybe we should try getting the foundational paper of that architecture and use that one to work, only bring more if there are some which revolutionazed something really big about it."

## Papers affected
None excluded or re-screened. Variants of families already covered move from "read next" to "deferred" in the coverage of SQ1–SQ5; they stay counted as found.
EOF
